title: What the Brier score is made of
subtitle: Reliability, resolution and uncertainty in CourtVision's MLB and international-soccer forecasts, checked against the closing market
abstract: CourtVision splits each in-game win-probability Brier score into three Murphy components -- reliability, resolution and uncertainty -- and stores both a directly computed Brier and a reconstructed Brier evaluated on the file's own 10 bins. This paper reports that split, and the signed remainder between the two Brier figures, for the two sports murphy_decomposition.json scores on both a model probability and a market-implied probability: MLB moneyline (78,986 rows) and international soccer moneyline (9,003 rows); no other sport appears in the artifact. In MLB the remainders are small and opposite in sign: direct minus reconstructed is +0.000518 for the model (0.237684 against 0.237166) and -0.000377 for the market (0.206653 against 0.207030). Model reliability (0.012701) is near market reliability (0.006061, a difference of +0.0066) while model resolution (0.023628) trails market resolution (0.047124, a difference of -0.0235), so the resolution term carries almost all of the 0.031031 Brier difference and the reliability term carries little of it. In international soccer both remainders are large and negative: -0.065642 for the model (0.227887 against 0.293529) and -0.066812 for the market (0.142726 against 0.209538). The artifact carries no second bin count and no per-bin residual, so nothing here identifies what produces them. MLB Brier Skill Score against the market is negative at every published grain, most negative late (-0.4635, n=13,981). Status: the MLB corpus behind both artifacts is contaminated, so the MLB conclusions are withdrawn pending regeneration and kept as a dated record.

blocks.text: CourtVision's in-game win-probability model returns a worse Brier score than the closing market in every sport where both sides' probabilities are scored on the same resolved games. The Murphy decomposition splits that score into three terms that add back to it: reliability (a penalty for a forecast curve that departs from the 45-degree line), resolution (a bonus for separating winners from losers) and uncertainty (the outcome's own base-rate variance). It says which term carries a difference arithmetically, not what causes the difference. murphy_decomposition.json carries that split for two sports -- MLB moneyline (78,986 rows) and international soccer moneyline (9,003 rows) -- and no others.

Before reading what the split says about MLB and soccer, this paper checks whether the split's own arithmetic closes: does reliability minus resolution plus uncertainty reproduce the directly computed Brier it is built beside. Only then does it read which component each sport's difference against the market sits in, and it separately reads brier_skill_scores.json to see whether the market's advantage is steady across the game or concentrated in one part of it.

murphy_decomposition.json stores one object per sport under sports.<sport>, each with a model_prob block and a market_prob block. Each block carries n (rows scored), brier (the directly computed mean squared error of that probability against the 0/1 outcome), reliability, resolution, uncertainty, and reconstructed_brier -- the file's own reconstruction of the Brier from its 10 probability bins. The file's method field states the identity as 'Brier = reliability - resolution + uncertainty'; reconstructed_brier is that right-hand side evaluated on the file's own bins, not a number this paper derives.

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.text: Reliability is the mean squared distance between each bin's average forecast and that bin's actual outcome frequency -- higher means the forecast curve is further off the diagonal. Resolution is how much of the outcome's variance the bins explain beyond the corpus base rate -- higher means the forecast separates winners from losers more sharply. Uncertainty is the base-rate variance of the outcome itself, fixed by the corpus, not by the forecaster.

Because model_prob and market_prob in a given sport are scored on the identical set of resolved games, their uncertainty terms are identical by construction: 0.248092 for MLB, 0.238877 for soccer_intl. That match is a basic internal check on the file, not itself a finding.

brier_skill_scores.json reports the same two sports' Brier scores again, this time by game-phase grain, alongside a climatology reference (a constant sport-level base-rate forecast) and the standard skill-score formula BSS = 1 - Brier / Brier_ref. Its honest_note field states plainly that BSS against the market is near or below 0 across sports and checkpoints.

Dates: three different files stamp these modules and none of the stamps is a single collection date. For the decomposition there is no artifact date at all: public/data/showcase/murphy_decomposition.json carries neither generated_at nor as_of, site_manifest.json lists the murphy_decomposition module with as_of null -- date not published -- and the curated insights/murphy_decomposition.json file states its own as_of as the literal string 'unknown'. For the skill scores there are three: the showcase artifact brier_skill_scores.json carries generated_at 2026-07-25T11:12:35Z, which is when that artifact was produced; site_manifest.json publishes the module with as_of 2026-07-25T04:34:43Z; and the curated insights/brier_skill_scores.json file carries as_of 2026-07-24T01:08:43Z, the stamp on that written summary. The three span about a day, which is evidence of separate passes rather than one canonical timestamp.

Every number in the tables below is copied directly from the two named artifacts. Two derived quantities are computed here, and both are trivial differences of cited numbers, reported as such: remainder = brier - reconstructed_brier (the gap between the directly computed Brier and the identity's own reconstruction of it), and, in the skill-score table, the grain totals used to check whether the named grains sum to the all grain. The reliability_gap and resolution_gap figures quoted for MLB and soccer (model minus market) are not computed here; they are copied from murphy_decomposition.json's own verdict text, which already states them.

No re-binning, no re-scoring and no walk-forward re-estimation were performed. This paper describes what the two stored artifacts contain and checks whether the Murphy identity holds inside them; it does not re-derive the decomposition from raw forecast-outcome pairs.

blocks.label: Status
blocks.text: MLB conclusions withdrawn pending corpus correction. A join-integrity check measured 2026-09-16 found that 126 of the 227 MLB game files behind both artifacts carry ticks from more than one real game, and that 27,076 of 78,986 ticks (34.3 percent) sit in a segment labelled with another game's outcome. The MLB rows below are withdrawn as current results and kept as a dated record; the tables stay published so a regenerated corpus can be compared against them. The check found 1 of the 51 international-soccer files mixed, so the soccer rows are under review.
Table 1 gives the full decomposition for both sports and both sides, plus the remainder (brier minus reconstructed_brier) for each.

blocks.caption: Murphy decomposition by sport and side (source murphy_decomposition.json; date not published)
blocks.note: Remainder = brier - reconstructed_brier, a trivial difference of two cited fields. The mlb remainders are +0.000518 and -0.000377, small and opposite in sign; both soccer_intl remainders are near -0.066.

blocks.text: In MLB the two Brier figures nearly agree. The model's direct Brier (0.237684) minus its reconstructed Brier (0.237166) leaves a remainder of +0.000518; the market's direct Brier (0.206653) minus its reconstructed Brier (0.207030) leaves -0.000377. The two are small and opposite in sign, so the 10-bin reconstruction tracks each directly computed Brier closely enough to read its components. Model reliability (0.012701) is near market reliability (0.006061) -- a reliability_gap of +0.0066, copied from the file's own verdict text -- while model resolution (0.023628) trails market resolution (0.047124), a resolution_gap of -0.0235. The model's Brier sits 0.031031 above the market's, and in this arithmetic the resolution term carries almost all of that difference and the reliability term carries little of it. Which term a difference sits in is a statement about the decomposition, not about why the two forecasts differ.

In international soccer both remainders are large and negative. Direct minus reconstructed is -0.065642 for the model (0.227887 against 0.293529) and -0.066812 for the market (0.142726 against 0.209538); the two sit within 0.0012 of each other, so neither is specific to the model's probabilities. The artifact carries no second bin count and no per-bin residual, so nothing in it identifies what produces them. Soccer's model-side reliability (0.092837) is larger than its model-side resolution (0.038185), the reverse of the MLB ordering, where model resolution (0.023628) is larger than model reliability (0.012701). On the market side of soccer, resolution (0.082761) is larger than reliability (0.053423), matching the MLB ordering; it is specifically the soccer model curve where the ordering flips.

blocks.label: Caution
blocks.text: A remainder near -0.066 on both soccer curves means the reliability, resolution and uncertainty terms for soccer_intl should not be read as precisely as the MLB terms. The file carries one bin count and no per-bin residual, so this paper states the remainders and stops there rather than naming a cause for them.

blocks.caption: MLB and soccer_intl 10-bin reliability curves (mean forecast vs observed outcome rate), model_prob and market_prob, the same bins the reliability and resolution terms in Table 1 are built from.

blocks.text: Brier = reliability - resolution + uncertainty; reconstructed_brier = reliability - resolution + uncertainty (evaluated on the file's 10 bins); remainder = brier - reconstructed_brier

brier_skill_scores.json breaks the same MLB corpus into three named game-phase grains -- early(inn1-3), mid(inn4-6), late(inn7+) -- alongside the all grain. Table 2 gives the Brier for model, market and climatology at each grain, plus both skill scores.

blocks.caption: MLB Brier Skill Score by grain, model vs climatology and model vs market (source brier_skill_scores.json, as of 2026-07-25)
blocks.note: BSS = 1 - Brier / Brier_ref; positive beats the reference, negative loses to it. Do not rank the all row against the three named grains below it -- see caution below.

blocks.text: The model beats the climatology reference at every grain (BSS model vs climatology positive throughout, from +0.0109 early to +0.1431 mid), which is the expected result for any in-game model against a constant base rate. Against the market the model loses at every grain, and the loss grows late: BSS model vs market is -0.0794 early, -0.1547 mid, and -0.4635 late, where the market's Brier (0.159878) sits furthest ahead of the model's (0.233989, a difference of 0.074111). This sits alongside the Table 1 arithmetic, in which the MLB difference is carried by the resolution term rather than the reliability term. Neither table tests a mechanism: Table 1 says which component the difference sits in, Table 2 says where in the game it is largest, and neither says what produces it.

blocks.label: Caution
blocks.text: The three named grains do not sum to the all grain: 19,900 + 18,765 + 13,981 = 52,646 rows, against 78,986 in all -- a shortfall of 26,340 rows that carry no early/mid/late label. All is the full corpus, not the sum of the three named grains, so it should not be read as a fourth row to rank alongside them; it is the aggregate they are a subset of.

sections.heading: Robustness and what would falsify this

items: If a wider MLB corpus (more than the current 78,986 rows) produced a materially larger remainder than the current +0.000518 (model) and -0.000377 (market), that would undercut trust in the 10-bin identity generally, not only for the smaller soccer sample.

If a finer bin scheme closed soccer's roughly -0.066 remainders on both curves, the remainders would be a property of the binning; this file carries one bin count (10), so that test cannot be run here.

If the soccer model's reliability-above-resolution ordering (0.092837 vs 0.038185) reversed once the soccer corpus grew well past 9,003 rows, that would suggest the current ordering is itself a small-n artifact rather than a stable feature of the soccer forecast.

The late-game MLB BSS-vs-market figure (-0.4635, n=13,981) would be falsified as a genuine late-game pattern if a subsequent MLB pull showed the mid or early grain moving to a similarly negative value -- the current pattern is monotonic (early less negative than mid less negative than late) and that ordering is itself testable against new data.

murphy_decomposition.json covers only MLB moneyline and international-soccer moneyline; no NBA, tennis or WNBA rows exist in this artifact, so nothing here generalizes to those sports. The MLB corpus behind both artifacts failed a join-integrity check measured 2026-09-16 (126 of 227 game files mix ticks from more than one game; 27,076 of 78,986 ticks carry another game's label), so every MLB figure here is a withdrawn dated record, not a current measurement.
The 10-bin reconstruction leaves remainders near -0.066 on both soccer_intl curves, and the file carries no second bin count and no per-bin residual, so this paper cannot say what produces them.

Reliability, resolution and uncertainty describe an aggregate corpus, not a paired game-by-game comparison; nothing here matches individual model calls against individual market calls on the same row.
A resolution difference is an arithmetic contribution to the Brier difference, not a cause; nothing here identifies what produces it.

The early/mid/late grains in brier_skill_scores.json cover 52,646 of the all grain's 78,986 MLB rows (66.6 percent); the remaining rows are not represented in the per-phase view, so the phase-level story in Table 2 is built on a subset of the rows behind Table 1's aggregate MLB numbers.

as_of dates differ across the artifacts describing these same modules (site_manifest.json's module dates versus the curated insights files' own as_of fields), so exact generation timestamps should not be treated as a single precise collection date.

sections.heading: How to read this on the site

blocks.text: The reliability curves behind Table 1 and the figure above are rendered in the score-decomposition inspector, which draws directly on the murphy_decomposition module. The calibration inspector carries the wider reliability-bin context these curves are built from. The cross-sport-comparability inspector is the right place to check, before comparing any number here across sports, whether MLB and soccer_intl are being compared on a like-for-like basis -- as this paper notes, they are not: the two corpora differ by nearly a factor of nine in size (78,986 vs 9,003 rows), and only these two sports carry a market-side decomposition at all.

Table 2's grain view and the brier_skill_scores module it is drawn from sit alongside this paper's decomposition table as a second way of looking at the same MLB difference: one by component (reliability against resolution), one by game phase (early, mid, late). Both locate the difference; neither explains it.
